hpi_details: 52F reports excruciating, sharp pain in her right heel when she takes her first steps out of bed in the morning. The pain improves gradually after walking around for 15 minutes but returns after sitting.
ideas: thinks she has a bone spur or heel strain
concerns: worried about walking and exercise limitation

teaching.one_liner: Degenerative microtearing of the plantar fascia causing intense heel pain on taking the first steps in the morning.

must_ask.say: Is the pain sharpest during the very first steps out of bed in the morning?
Does the pain ease off slightly as you walk around, but return after standing?
Is the pain located directly under the bottom inner side of your heel bone?
Have you recently increased running distance or changed to flat non-supportive shoes?
Do your calf muscles or back of ankle feel tight when stretching?

history.answer: Doctor, I have this awful sharp pain in my right heel whenever I take my first steps out of bed in the morning.
It started gradually about three weeks ago, but it has become much worse over the past week.
The pain is right under the bottom of my right heel, slightly toward the inner side, and it stays right there.
It feels like an excruciating, sharp stabbing pain, almost like stepping on a nail.
First thing in the morning it is easily an 8 out of 10, but later in the day it settles down to a 3 or 4.
The sharp pain lasts about fifteen minutes after I get out of bed before it starts easing up.
Walking around gently for about fifteen minutes actually loosens it up and makes it feel better, but prolonged standing makes it ache again by evening.
It is worst on the first steps in the morning, barefoot walking on hard floors, or standing up after sitting for a while.
Sitting down and resting off my feet relieves the sharp pain, and gentle walking gradually loosens it.
If I press right on the bottom inside corner of my heel bone, it is intensely tender.
Yes, my right calf and the back of my heel feel very tight and stiff, especially in the morning.
I haven't noticed any swelling, redness, or warmth in the heel or ankle.
No, I do not have any numbness, tingling, or burning sensations anywhere in my foot or toes.
I can bear weight and walk, though I limp during those initial steps because of the sharp heel pain.
No, I have not had any fever, chills, night sweats, or unexplained weight loss.
No, the pain does not wake me up from sleep at night.
No, there was no trip, fall, ankle sprain, or sudden pop.
I wear flat dress shoes with thin soles at school, and I recently increased my walking for exercise.
I had a mild ache in the same heel about two years ago, but it cleared up on its own.
I tried taking over-the-counter ibuprofen a couple of times and iced my heel, which helped a little.
It makes getting up in the morning dreadfully painful and makes it difficult to stand in front of my classroom all day.
I was wondering if I developed a bone spur on my heel or strained a ligament.
I am worried that this might permanently limit my ability to walk, exercise, and do my teaching job.
I would really like to learn proper heel stretches and see if orthotics or shoe inserts would fix this.
I struggle with being overweight, but I do not have diabetes, high blood pressure, or gout.
I have never had any surgeries or hospital stays.
I am not taking any regular prescription medications, only the occasional ibuprofen.
I do not have any allergies to medications or anything else.
I have never smoked in my life.
I only have an occasional glass of wine once or twice a month.
I work as an elementary school teacher, standing for long periods on hard floors, and I live with my husband.
There is no family history of joint diseases or inflammatory arthritis.
My periods became irregular last year and stopped completely six months ago; there is no chance of pregnancy.

exam.finding: Blood pressure 128/82 mmHg, pulse 72 beats per minute, respirations 16 breaths per minute, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Alert, well-appearing woman, overweight, sitting comfortably with no acute distress.

Marked point tenderness localized to the medial tubercle of the right calcaneus, with pain aggravated by passive dorsiflexion of the great toe; no joint effusion, erythema, or pain on calcaneal squeeze.
Tightness of the right Achilles tendon and calf muscles with limited ankle dorsiflexion; no tenderness, swelling, or palpable defect in the Achilles tendon.
Intact light touch sensation over the plantar surface and toes; negative Tinel sign behind the medial malleolus.
Dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses are 2+ and symmetric bilaterally with warm extremities.
Mild antalgic gait favoring the right heel on initial steps, improving with continued walking.
